newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico sees lower interest rates in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico sees lower interest rates in 1997.

text.p: Mexico's central bank expects interest rates to decline next year as inflation falls off, Banco de Mexico General Director of Economic Research Agustin Carstens said.
Carsten made his remarks on a conference call to analysts on Thursday to explain the central bank's 1997 monetary policy plan.
"In general, we expect interest rates, both nominal and real, to go down. I think this is probably the main result that we expect from our monetary program," he said.

"There are firm grounds to expect lower interest rates as we have seen in 1996. In 1996, basically the level of interest rates has been reduced by half while inflation will pretty much be reduced by half," Carstens said.
The main point of the central bank's monetary program released on Wednesday is an approximate 24.5 percent increase in the monetary base -- basically coins and bills -- during 1997 from this year.

The expected growth in the monetary base comes from expected real GDP growth of 4.5 percent, inflation of 15 percent, and a remonetization that is estimated at 3.6 percent of the amount of the base at the close of 1996. Remonetization occurs when people hold onto more cash as inflation slows.
Another important factor that could affect interest rates will be the trajectory of interest rates in the United States, he noted.
Carstens said that if the growth rate or the rate of remonetization is less than expected, the central bank will supply less money to the system.

"The 24.5 percent is an estimate. If during the year the demand for money or the remonetization is lower than the one implied by the 24.5 percent, we will supply a lesser amount of money, therefore the 24.5 percent rate of growth will not materialize," he said.
Carstens said the central bank expects to hit its inflation target of 15 percent in 1997, as factors that pressured prices this year subside.
He noted that at least two percentage points in 1996's inflation hike came from higher commodities prices, such as corn and beans.
A weakening in the peso in late 1995 also created more inflationary pressures than the central bank anticipated. A scheduled wage hike also came in higher than expected.
"Many of the conditions that we mentioned will not be present in 1997," he said. For example, the price of commodities such as corn have been coming down, he noted.
The central bank forecast inflation of 20.5 percent for 1996, but analysts expect it to come in closer to 26.5 percent.
Banco de Mexico plans to accumulate $1.9 billion in net international assets in 1997, and Carstens said that amount could increase.
He said that at least half of that increase will come from the exercise of the bank's dollar put option program.
"If the conditions are met and more of the options are being exercised, then certainly we think we can accumulate more than the $1.9 billion," he said.
The other half will come from routine transactions that the central bank conducts with the federal government and with Pemex, he said, but added that the amount could also increase.
"If the price of oil increases more or turns out to have a higher average for next year, we expect certainly to accumulate more international reserves," he said.
-- Robert Kozak, Mexico City newsroom (525) 728 9559.
